# Abstract {.unnumbered}

{{< include _abstract.qmd >}}

**Keywords** Job satisfaction; Non-cognitive skills; Big Five personality; Working conditions; Occupational inequality; Cross-national comparison; PIAAC

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Two employees do the same job for the same pay and rate it differently. Job satisfaction is one of the main indicators through which statistical offices, international organizations, and employers assess the quality of working life [@cazes2015], whereas some scholars even treat it as one of the main components of subjective well-being [@sousa-poza2000; @vanpraag2003; @judgeklinger2008; @bowling2010]. These ratings also reflect workers' dispositions. The OECD's analysis of the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) finds that emotionally stable and extraverted adults are more satisfied with their jobs in nearly every participating country, and these associations "persist, albeit weaker" after accounting for wages, sector, and occupation [@oecd2025, p. 69]. If workers are more satisfied because they hold better jobs, satisfaction still measures the job. If personality affects how workers view and describe the same job, their ratings also reflect temperament. The distinction matters because job satisfaction is often read as evidence of job quality, while the same score may combine the conditions of a job with the worker's way of evaluating them.

Economists have estimated the wage returns to personality traits and their payoff in employment and occupation [@heckman2006; @almlund2011; @cobbclarkschurer2012]. Human capital theory treats personality traits as non-cognitive skills with a productive role [@humphries2017]. In the definition of @green2013, skills are productive, socially determined, and expandable through training and development. @cunha2007 model how such skills are produced over the life cycle, with skills acquired early raising the productivity of later investment (dynamic complementarity). Job satisfaction rarely appears in this body of work, although it predicts quitting and @freeman1978 treated it as an economic variable. Psychological and OECD studies of the personality gradient in satisfaction [@judge2002; @oecd2025] do not compare subjective and objective rewards in the same data. They also do not test why a trait is associated with higher satisfaction. The source of this established correlation between personality and job satisfaction is not yet clear.

The study uses PIAAC data from `r nC` high-income countries to examine the sources of the satisfaction premium and contributes to the literature in 3 ways. First, the subjective reward to non-cognitive skills is measured with the same instrument across national contexts. The *subjective reward* is defined as the association between a trait and job satisfaction at a given level of pay and background characteristics, and pay itself is the objective reward. Second, the study tests whether the premium reflects sorting into better jobs or a different view of the same job. Workers with productive non-cognitive skills may hold better jobs (*exposure*), respond differently to the same working conditions (*reactivity*), or report the same conditions differently (*appraisal*) [@bolger1995]. Earlier studies tested these routes only with diary data from single organizations and could not show whether workers with different traits hold different jobs. Finally, I estimate what the satisfaction gap between high and low occupational groups would be if the groups did not differ in personality profiles. This counterfactual gap splits the observed gap into the part accounted for by non-cognitive skills and the part accounted for by pay and working conditions.

Causal mediation analysis [@imai2010] is combined with a comparison of workers in the same job, defined by occupation and industry within each country. The mediation analysis gives the share of each premium that varies with pay, objective job characteristics, and reported conditions. The within-job comparison is used to test whether the traits are associated with the jobs themselves or with how workers report them. The main outcome is whether a worker is extremely satisfied, the top category of the scale. A separate test asks at which end of the scale each trait acts. The premiums are tested against omitted-variable bias [@oster2019], and the mediated parts are tested against unobserved confounding [@imai2010b]. To check whether the premiums reflect only a general tendency to report one's life favorably, I also hold life satisfaction fixed.

On average, `r pc(vs_mean)`% of employees are extremely satisfied with their jobs. One standard deviation of emotional stability raises this probability by `r pp(tmean("EMOS"))` percentage points, and extraversion by `r pp(tmean("EXTR"))`. The effect of agreeableness is `r pp(tmean("AGRE"))` points. Conscientiousness has a smaller effect, significant in `r tsig("CONS")` of `r nC` countries, and open-mindedness in `r tsig("OPEM")`. Pay carries `r pc(payshare("EMOS"))`% of the emotional-stability effect. Pay, job characteristics, job demands, job resources, and skill underuse together carry `r pc(medshare("EMOS"))`%, and the rest is direct. The traits act at different ends of the scale. Emotional stability mainly lowers the probability of being neutral or dissatisfied, while extraversion mainly raises the probability of being extremely satisfied. Workers with different traits hold similar jobs but report them differently. Within the same occupation and industry, less stable workers report more demands and also more resources than their colleagues. The premium is concentrated in low depression. Personality composition accounts for about `r pc(median(abs(gap_change("raw", "standardised")) / abs(gap("raw")$estimate)))`% of the satisfaction gap between high and low occupational groups.

The results matter for the use of job satisfaction as a quality-of-life indicator. Satisfaction gaps between groups of workers are often read as gaps in job quality, for example between women and men [@clark1997]. If part of satisfaction reflects how people appraise their jobs, these gaps also reflect who the workers are. Where personality is measured, researchers can estimate this component alongside the gap.

# Background and hypotheses {#sec-hyp}

Organizational psychology established that job attitudes have a dispositional component. Workers' satisfaction persists across job changes [@staw1985]. In the meta-analysis of @judge2002, the Big Five correlate with satisfaction at 0.29 for emotional stability, 0.26 for conscientiousness, 0.25 for extraversion, 0.17 for agreeableness, and 0.02 for openness. Because these estimates do not hold pay or occupation fixed, they cannot show whether satisfied workers earn more or hold better jobs. They also do not show how the association arises.

With the 2023 Survey of Adult Skills, the OECD extended the descriptive evidence across countries [@oecd2025]. In its estimates, a 1-standard-deviation increase in emotional stability is associated with a 6-percentage-point higher probability of high job satisfaction, and extraversion with 4 points, which is comparable to literacy. After accounting for wages and job characteristics, the association with literacy is no longer significant, whereas the associations with personality remain. The report interprets this as person–environment fit [@kristofbrown2005], or as emotion regulation, without testing either explanation. A recent study of young workers in 1 country also finds that the premium remains after controlling for wages and job characteristics [@avanesian2026]. These studies do not compare subjective and objective rewards. In the theory of compensating differentials [@rosen1986], a trait associated with satisfaction that the market does not pay for raises a further question. The question is whether workers with the trait hold better jobs or experience the same job differently.

@bolger1995 distinguish differential *exposure* to stressors from differential *reactivity* to them. A third route, differential *appraisal*, comes from @watson1984 on negative affectivity and refers to the tendency to report the same situation differently. In diary studies and single organizations, where these routes were tested, the same person reports both stressors and strain. Some studies therefore partial out negative affectivity as a nuisance, while others treat it as a cause [@spector2000]. Representative data with occupation codes allow each worker's report of a condition to be compared with the average report of workers in the same occupation and industry. Measurement choices of this kind have been linked to quitting [@pelly2023] and job-quality rankings [@stephens2025].

> **H1 (Subjective reward).** Holding pay fixed, emotional stability, extraversion, and agreeableness are associated with higher job satisfaction. The direction for conscientiousness and open-mindedness is unclear; their bivariate correlations are positive [@judge2002], but their adjusted associations vary across countries [@oecd2025].

The first route is *exposure*. The job demands–resources model describes job quality through 2 groups of conditions [@karasek1979; @bakker2007]. Demands such as time pressure, repetitive or physically strenuous work, and constant change drain workers. Resources such as autonomy and learning, or support and voice, motivate them. Emotionally stable workers may avoid high-strain jobs, and extraverts may find jobs with more contact and autonomy. If so, part of the premium moves with job conditions.

> **H2 (Exposure).** Part of the association between personality and satisfaction moves with reported working conditions. Emotional stability is associated with lower reported demands (H2a). Extraversion is associated with more resources, particularly autonomy and voice, as well as learning and social tasks (H2b).

The second route is *appraisal*. Negative affectivity is the core of low emotional stability. It colors reports of both stressors and satisfaction [@watson1984], and dispositional affect persists in job attitudes over long periods [@staw1985; @judge2001]. Under this account, traits predict how workers *report* their conditions relative to others in the same job, while the conditions themselves do not differ. The premium should then be concentrated in the affective component of the trait. Appraisal and sorting also make different predictions. A worker in a worse job than colleagues should report higher demands and fewer resources. A worker for whom the same work feels like more of everything should report more demands and also more resources.

> **H3 (Appraisal).** (a) Trait associations with reported conditions are concentrated in workers' deviations from their occupational-group means and are small in the group means. The part of the premium that moves with conditions moves with the deviations. Emotional stability predicts lower reports of demands and resources. (b) Within emotional stability, the premium is carried mainly by low depression. The difference between the depression and anxiety coefficients is distinguishable from zero.

The third route is *reactivity*. Trait activation theory holds that a trait matters where the situation calls for it [@tett2003]. Emotional stability should cushion the cost of demands, and social tasks should reward extraverts. Learning should reward the open-minded, and underuse should frustrate them. Autonomy should matter more to the conscientious, and support should matter more to the agreeable.

> **H4 (Reactivity).** Traits moderate the association between job conditions and satisfaction. Emotional stability weakens the cost of time pressure, repetitive work, and change (H4a). Extraversion strengthens the benefit of social tasks (H4b). Openness strengthens the benefit of learning and the cost of skill underuse (H4c). Conscientiousness strengthens the benefit of autonomy (H4d). Agreeableness strengthens the benefit of support (H4e).

Personality affects satisfaction comparisons between groups of workers only when the groups differ enough in personality composition, regardless of the route. Managers and professionals are on average more emotionally stable and extraverted than workers in operative and elementary occupations. Their satisfaction gap should therefore narrow when both groups have the same personality distribution. I chose this comparison before seeing the result. It is the widest contrast in occupational skill level that still leaves enough employees in each group in most countries.

> **H5 (Composition).** Within each country, the satisfaction gap between the high occupational group (ISCO 1–2) and the low one (ISCO 8–9) narrows when both groups are standardized to a common personality distribution. It narrows further when pay and reported conditions are adjusted for.

The 5 hypotheses run from reward size to its consequences. H1 concerns reward size. H2 to H4 concern its source, and H5 concerns its consequences for comparisons between groups of workers.

A further question concerns the end of the satisfaction scale at which a trait acts. Neuroticism, the opposite pole of emotional stability, is linked mainly to negative affect, and extraversion mainly to positive affect [@costa1980; @watson1984]. If the emotional-stability premium works through negative affect, emotional stability should mainly lower the probability of being neutral or dissatisfied. Extraversion should mainly raise the probability of being extremely satisfied. I added this test during revision, after the main outcome was set to the top category, so it is not one of the 5 hypotheses.

# Data {#sec-data}

I use the public-use files of the second cycle of PIAAC, fielded in 2022–2023 in representative samples of adults [@oecd2024]. Employed respondents rate their satisfaction with their current job on a 5-point scale. Most employees are satisfied: on average `r pc(vs_mean)`% choose the top category, extremely satisfied (`r pc(min(S$desc$very_satisfied))`% to `r pc(max(S$desc$very_satisfied))`% by country), and only `r pc(min(ns_share))`% to `r pc(max(ns_share))`% are neutral or dissatisfied (Appendix, Table A1). The main outcome is a binary indicator for being extremely satisfied. The 3 lowest categories form a second binary outcome, *not satisfied*, and the 1–5 score is used in robustness checks (@sec-threats). The Big Five are measured with the 15-item BFI-2-XS and released as national z-scores, so a coefficient is the change in the probability of being extremely satisfied per within-country standard deviation of the trait. In `r n_fac` countries, the 30-item BFI-2-S is also released, with 3 facets per trait [@soto2017]. The sample covers employees aged 25–65 in the `r nC` countries that release these variables. Samples and module coverage by country are in Table A2. Pay is the within-country decile of hourly earnings including bonuses, released for employees in `r n_pay` of the `r nC` countries. `r flagname` do not release an employee earnings measure. These 3 countries enter without the pay block and are marked with † in all figures. Respondents with a missing decile in a pay country are kept with a missing-pay indicator; complete-case results are in Table A19.

The mediator variables are listed in Appendix Table A3. Because the appraisal hypothesis concerns the gap between a job and its report, I use the workers' own reports of working conditions. Background controls are age band, sex, education, birthplace, parental education, and numeracy (mean of the 10 plausible values). Occupation, contract type, weekly hours, firm size, sector, supervisory duties, and tenure enter the mediation model as a block of job characteristics. PIAAC does not record union membership, job security, commuting time, or shift work.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-desc
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive statistics of the analysis sample by country (weighted)"
DS <- S$desc[order(cname[S$desc$country]), ]
tab <- data.frame(Country = ifelse(DS$country %in% flag, paste0(cname[DS$country], " †"), cname[DS$country]), N = big(DS$n),
  `Women (%)` = pc(DS$women), `Tertiary (%)` = pc(DS$tertiary), Numeracy = sprintf("%.0f", DS$numeracy),
  `Extremely satisfied (%)` = pc(DS$very_satisfied), `Not satisfied (%)` = pc(DS$not_satisfied), `Satisfaction (1–5)` = f2(DS$satisfaction),
  `Time pressure (1–5)` = f2(DS$time_pressure), `Autonomy (1–5)` = f2(DS$autonomy), `Skill underuse (%)` = pc(DS$underuse),
  `Support and voice` = ifelse(DS$extended, "Yes", "No"), check.names = FALSE)
fin(kb(tab, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrrrrrrrc"), size = 7, "Source: PIAAC Cycle 2 public-use files (OECD, 2024). Employees aged 25–65. Weighted with the final survey weight; N is the unweighted analysis sample. Numeracy: mean of the 10 plausible values (0–500 scale). Extremely satisfied: top category of the 5-point scale (main outcome). Not satisfied: neither satisfied nor dissatisfied, dissatisfied, or extremely dissatisfied. Time pressure and autonomy are the raw item scales; skill underuse is the share reporting skills higher than the job requires. Support and voice: the extended module is fielded. † No earnings decile released.")
```

# Empirical strategy {#sec-strategy}

## Identification strategy {#sec-ident}

Every model is estimated separately in each country and weighted with the final survey weight. Countries are not pooled. For employee $i$, the baseline equation

$$
S_i = \alpha + \sum_{k=1}^{5} \tau_k T_{ik} + X_i'\gamma + u_i
$$ {#eq-total}

gives the *total effect* $\tau_k$ of trait $k$. Here $S_i$ equals 1 if the employee is extremely satisfied and 0 otherwise, so @eq-total is a linear probability model and $\tau_k$ is a change in probability. $T_{ik}$ are the 5 traits, entered jointly as national z-scores, and $X_i$ are the background controls: age band, sex, education, birthplace, parental education, and numeracy. Pay, the job, and its conditions are left out of $X_i$ on purpose. Workers with different traits may earn more or hold different jobs, so these variables enter as mediators. The total effect is the difference in the probability of being extremely satisfied between workers 1 standard deviation apart in a trait who have the same other traits and background. Tables A6 to A8 give every coefficient of @eq-total in each country.

*Mediation model.* The mediators form 5 blocks (@fig-schematic):

1. *Pay*: the within-country earnings decile.
2. *Job characteristics*: occupation, contract type, weekly hours (5 bands), firm size, public or private sector, supervisory duties, and tenure with the employer (5 bands). These are the objective job characteristics that economic studies of job satisfaction hold fixed [@clark1997; @hamermesh2001].
3. *Job demands*: time pressure, repetitive tasks, physical work, and change in the work environment.
4. *Job resources*: autonomy, learning, and social tasks, as well as support and voice in the `r n_ext` countries that measure them.
5. *Skill underuse*: skills higher than the job requires, entered with the opposite mismatch and a missing category.

I follow the linear structural equation approach of @imai2010, extended to several mediators by @imai2013. Each mediator variable $M_{im}$ is regressed on the traits and $X_i$ (mediator equations, coefficient $a_{km}$ on $T_{ik}$). The satisfaction indicator is regressed on the traits, $X_i$, and all mediators at once (outcome equation, coefficient $b_m$ on $M_{im}$ and $c'_k$ on $T_{ik}$; every coefficient in Tables A9 to A11). The *average causal mediation effect* (ACME) of trait $k$ through block $j$ is the sum, over the mediators in that block, of the products of the 2 coefficients:

$$
\delta_{kj} = \sum_{m \in j} a_{km} b_m .
$$ {#eq-acme}

The coefficient $c'_k$ is the *average direct effect* (ADE): the difference between workers with the same pay, job characteristics, demands, resources, and skill match. With linear equations, the effects add up:

$$
\tau_k = c'_k + \sum_{j=1}^{5} \delta_{kj}, \qquad \tau_k^{\text{net}} = \tau_k - \delta_{k,\text{pay}} .
$$ {#eq-additive}

The premium *net of pay*, $\tau_k^{\text{net}}$, is the total effect minus the ACME through pay, and H1 concerns it. All ACMEs come from the same outcome equation, so they do not depend on the order of the blocks. In the mediation package, each block enters as a single index $H_{ij} = M_{ij}'b_j$, its fitted contribution in the outcome equation. The ACME through $H_{ij}$ equals $\delta_{kj}$, and the 5 block ACMEs add up to the ACME through the sum of the indices. A missing condition is set to 0 with an indicator in its block, and a missing decile is set to the country mean with an indicator. In the `r nC - n_pay` countries without earnings deciles, the model has 4 blocks.

```{r}
#| label: fig-schematic
#| fig-cap: "The mediation model. A trait affects satisfaction directly (average direct effect, ADE) and through each mediator block (average causal mediation effect, ACME). For H3, the blocks of job demands and job resources are further split into the occupational-group mean and the worker's deviation from it."
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-width: 7
draw_schematic()
```

*Group mean and deviation.* H3 asks whether a trait goes with the job or with its report. For each reported condition, I compute the weighted mean report of the other workers in the same group. A group is a country × the finest released occupation × an industry section, and where it has fewer than 10 other members, the occupation alone. The worker's deviation is the own report minus this leave-one-out group mean, so the 2 parts add up to the report. Without employer-level data, occupation-by-industry groups are the closest available reference point for the conditions attached to a type of work. The mediation model is then re-estimated with the demands block split into 2 blocks, the group means and the deviations, and the resources block split in the same way. The ACME through demands thus becomes a part through the group means plus a part through the deviations. Workers in a group can still hold different jobs, so the deviation contains real differences in conditions as well as the worker's reporting style. The split shows where the trait associations lie, but it cannot by itself separate the view of a job from unmeasured differences between jobs. Weighted regressions of each part on the traits and controls give the trait coefficients on the group means and on the deviations. The coefficients on the group means are tested for *equivalence* to zero with 2 one-sided tests and a margin of `r eq_margin_cell` SD, less than half the typical coefficient on the deviations. Tables A4 and A5 report the group definitions and re-estimates with stricter groups.

*Where on the scale.* For the test of where each trait acts, I add 2 coefficients from @eq-total with the pay decile as a control: the effect on the probability of being extremely satisfied and the effect on the probability of being not satisfied. Their sum is the coefficient in a regression of the indicator "extremely satisfied or not satisfied" on the same variables, which gives its standard error directly. A positive sum means that the trait raises the top more than it lowers the bottom. An ordered probit provides the benchmark. With a single latent index, every trait shifts the whole distribution, so the ratio of the effect at the bottom to the effect at the top is the same for all traits in a country. I compare each trait's observed sum with the sum implied by the ordered probit (@sec-asym).

*Which method answers which question.* The mediation package estimates every quantity that runs from a trait through a variable to satisfaction: the total effect, the 5 block ACMEs, the ADE, the ACMEs through group means and deviations, and their sensitivity to confounding. The other questions do not concern such paths, so they use weighted least squares with conventional standard errors. These are the trait coefficients on the group means and deviations (H3a), the facet coefficients (H3b), the trait × condition products (H4), the standardized occupational gap (H5), the test of where on the scale a trait acts, and the robustness checks. For H3b, each trait is replaced with its 3 facets in the `r n_fac` countries that release them, and the depression–anxiety difference is tested directly.

For H4, the 8 hypothesized products and 3 placebo products with no proposed mechanism are added to each country's model with all conditions. Traits are centered and conditions standardized, so each product is the change in a condition's slope per standard deviation of the trait. A product within ±`r pp(eq_margin_int)` percentage points of zero, about half the slope of autonomy, learning, or voice, is treated as equivalent to zero. Cross-sectional interactions compare different workers in different conditions, so they say little about how a single worker would react to a change.

For H5, 2 groups are compared in each country. The high group is managers and professionals (ISCO 1–2). The low group is plant and machine operators and workers in elementary occupations (ISCO 8–9). Where only the 4-level occupational skill variable is released, its top and bottom levels are compared. The satisfaction indicator is regressed on the 5 traits separately in each group, and each group's mean is predicted at the pooled trait distribution. The difference between the 2 predictions is the gap that would remain if both groups had the same personality composition and kept their own trait coefficients. The further gaps add the pay decile and then the reported conditions, with common slopes.

The intervals of the mediation estimates are quasi-Bayesian approximations from `r big(med_info$sims)` draws [@imai2010]. Numeracy, literacy, and problem solving enter as the mean of their 10 plausible values. Each figure shows the country estimates and their mean across countries, which keeps the effects additive. The text reports significance from each country's own test. Counts after the Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment for multiple testing [@benjamini1995] are at the end of the Appendix.

The study follows the principles of literate statistical computing [@knuth1984]. The manuscript is written in Quarto [@allaire2024] with R [@rcore2025], and every number, table, and figure is computed from the public-use files by the code that accompanies it. The mediation estimates and their sensitivity analysis are outputs of the mediation package [version `r med_info$version`, @tingley2014].

## Methodological threats {#sec-threats}

A causal reading of the ACMEs and the ADE requires sequential ignorability [@imai2010]. Given the controls, the traits must be independent of potential satisfaction and of the mediators. Given the traits and controls, the mediators must be independent of potential satisfaction. With several blocks, no block may confound the effects through another [@imai2013]. Cross-sectional data cannot secure these conditions, but they permit partial checks of 5 threats.

*Outcome scale.* The satisfaction item has 5 ordered categories. Treating such scores as cardinal is standard practice in the economics of job satisfaction [@freeman1978; @clarkoswald1996; @clark1997; @hamermesh2001; @card2012]. @ferrerfrijters2004 show that assuming cardinality or ordinality matters little for the estimated determinants of satisfaction, and @kaiseroswald2022 find that reported feelings relate to later decisions, such as quitting a job, in a way that is fairly close to linear. @bondlang2019 show, however, that the sign of a difference in mean satisfaction between groups can reverse under a monotone transformation of the underlying scale. The main outcome avoids this problem. A binary indicator for the top category uses only the order of the categories and needs no assumption about the distances between them. Because most employees are satisfied, the top category also separates them where the scale has most of its variation. I estimate it as a linear probability model because the effects then add up (@eq-additive). In logit or probit models, the coefficients change scale when mediators are added, so the total effect does not split into its parts. An ordered model in the mediation would also impose a single index, under which every trait shifts the whole distribution, and @sec-asym shows that the traits act at different ends of the scale. Four checks use other forms of the outcome (Table A18): the mediation model for not satisfied, the same model for the 1–5 score treated as cardinal, ordered-probit effects on the probabilities of the top and the bottom categories without and with all mediator variables, and logit marginal effects.

*Common-method reporting.* The same person reports traits, conditions, and satisfaction at the same time. A passing mood or a general disposition to describe one's situation favorably would raise both the reported conditions and satisfaction, which violates sequential ignorability. H3 tests for this disposition, and a further model holds life satisfaction fixed.

*Unobserved confounding.* For the mediators, the sensitivity analysis of @imai2010b takes each cumulative set of blocks as a single mediator. It gives ρ*, the correlation between the errors of the mediator and outcome equations at which the ACME is zero. For the traits, I estimate the coefficient that would remain if unobservables mattered as much as the observed controls [@oster2019].

*Reverse causality.* Personality is measured in adulthood together with the job, so the job may have shaped the trait reports. Adult personality is fairly stable [@cobbclarkschurer2012]. If jobs gradually shaped trait reports, the trait associations would grow with tenure, and trait × long-tenure products test for this gradient. An immediate effect of the job on trait reports would not show in this test.

*Measurement error.* Each trait is measured with 3 items, which attenuates the premiums. In the `r n_fac` countries that also release 6-item scores, the premiums are re-estimated with the longer scales.

# Results {#sec-results}

## The subjective reward to non-cognitive skills {#sec-h1}

@fig-h1 shows the total effect of each trait by country. At the same education, background, and numeracy, 1 standard deviation of emotional stability raises the probability of being extremely satisfied by `r pp(tmean("EMOS"))` percentage points (range `r rng(100 * TOT$estimate[TOT$var == "EMOS"], 1)`), from a mean of `r pc(vs_mean)`%. The effect is significant at the 5% level in `r tsig("EMOS")` of `r nC` countries. Table A12 gives the country estimates. The total effect of extraversion is `r pp(tmean("EXTR"))` points (significant in `r tsig("EXTR")` countries) and that of agreeableness `r pp(tmean("AGRE"))` (`r tsig("AGRE")` countries). Conscientiousness has a smaller effect, `r pp(tmean("CONS"))` points (`r tsig("CONS")` countries), and open-mindedness `r pp(tmean("OPEM"))` (`r tsig("OPEM")` countries). The sizes are close to the OECD's adjusted estimates on the same survey for high job satisfaction [@oecd2025]. The ordering differs from the bivariate correlations of @judge2002, where conscientiousness ranks second.

Little of the premium comes through pay. The ACME through the earnings decile is `r pp(amean("pay", "EMOS"), 2)` points for emotional stability, `r pc(payshare("EMOS"))`% of the total effect in the `r n_pay` countries with deciles, and it is significant in `r npos("pay", "EMOS")` of them. Net of pay, the premium is `r pp(netpay("EMOS"))` points for emotional stability, `r pp(netpay("EXTR"))` for extraversion, and `r pp(netpay("AGRE"))` for agreeableness. In the weighted regressions with the pay decile as a control (Table A13), adding occupation changes the coefficients by `r pct1(occ_absorb("EMOS"))`% for emotional stability, `r pct1(occ_absorb("EXTR"))`% for extraversion, and `r pct1(occ_absorb("AGRE"))`% for agreeableness. With log hourly earnings instead of deciles, in the `r n_lw` countries that release them, the mean emotional-stability coefficient is `r pp(kmean("EMOS", KLW))` points against `r pp(kmean("EMOS", KDW))`. The difference in the probability of being extremely satisfied between the top and the bottom earnings decile in the same model is `r pp(mean(PC$top_vs_bottom))` points on average across the `r nrow(PC)` countries with pay data. The emotional-stability coefficient per standard deviation is therefore about `r pc(mean(PC$emos) / mean(PC$top_vs_bottom))`% of the within-country pay gradient in satisfaction. The comparison uses 2 coefficients from the same model and sample and gives no monetary value.

The evidence for H1 is strong for emotional stability, extraversion, and agreeableness. Their total effects are significant in `r tsig("EMOS")`, `r tsig("EXTR")`, and `r tsig("AGRE")` of `r nC` countries, and emotional stability lowers the probability of being not satisfied in all `r with_med("not_satisfied", tneg("EMOS"))` (@sec-asym). The evidence for conscientiousness is moderate. Its total effect is positive in `r tposn("CONS")` of `r nC` countries and significant at the 5% level in `r tsig("CONS")`: `r tnames("CONS")`. Only in `r tnames("CONS", -1)` is it negative and significant. The evidence for open-mindedness is limited. Its total effect is positive and significant in `r tsig("OPEM")` countries, `r tnames("OPEM")`, and `r if (tneg("OPEM") == 0) "negative and significant in none" else paste("negative and significant in", tnames("OPEM", -1))`. The labor markets in which conscientious or open-minded workers are more satisfied differ, and the cross-country means of `r pp(tmean("CONS"))` and `r pp(tmean("OPEM"))` points conceal this variation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-h1
#| fig-cap: "Total effect of each trait on the probability of being extremely satisfied, by country. Estimates from mediate(): percentage points per standard deviation of the trait, at the same education, background and numeracy; 95% intervals. Filled: p < 0.05; grey: p < 0.10; hollow: neither. Bottom row: mean across countries with 95% interval. † No earnings decile released."
#| fig-height: 7.2
#| fig-width: 12
u <- TOT[, c("country", "var", "estimate", "se", "lower", "upper", "p")]; u[c("estimate", "se", "lower", "upper")] <- 100 * u[c("estimate", "se", "lower", "upper")]; u$panel <- tl[u$var]
fig_country_dots(u, tl, cname, flag, "Total effect per SD of the trait (percentage points), 95% interval")
```

## Where on the scale: emotional stability at the bottom, extraversion at the top {#sec-asym}

@tbl-asym compares the effect of each trait on the probability of being extremely satisfied with its effect on the probability of being not satisfied. Emotional stability lowers the probability of being not satisfied by `r pp(-with_med("not_satisfied", tmean("EMOS")))` percentage points, significantly in all `r with_med("not_satisfied", tneg("EMOS"))` countries, from a mean of `r pc(mean(S$desc$not_satisfied))`%. This is more than its effect at the top, `r pp(tmean("EMOS"))` points. Extraversion has the reverse pattern. It raises the top by `r pp(tmean("EXTR"))` points but lowers the bottom by only `r pp(-with_med("not_satisfied", tmean("EXTR")))`, significant in `r with_med("not_satisfied", tneg("EXTR"))` countries. The ratio of the bottom effect to the top effect is `r f2(bt_ratio("EMOS"))` for emotional stability and `r f2(bt_ratio("EXTR"))` for extraversion. The ordered probit, which forces both traits to shift the whole distribution, implies a ratio of about `r f2(ord_ratio("EMOS"))` for each. Agreeableness lies close to the ordered-probit benchmark (`r f2(bt_ratio("AGRE"))` against `r f2(ord_ratio("AGRE"))`). Conscientiousness acts mainly at the top (`r f2(bt_ratio("CONS"))`). It lowers the probability of being not satisfied in only `r with_med("not_satisfied", tneg("CONS"))` countries, which is why its evidence is stronger for the top category than for the 1–5 score.

The country tests agree. For emotional stability, the sum of the top and bottom effects is below the sum implied by the ordered probit in `r tb_below("EMOS")` of `r nC` countries, and significantly negative in `r tb("EMOS", -1)`. For extraversion, it is above the implied sum in `r tb_above("EXTR")` countries and significantly positive in `r tb("EXTR", 1)`, never significantly negative. Emotional stability thus works mainly by keeping workers out of the neutral and dissatisfied categories, and extraversion by moving them into the top one. This pattern matches the link of neuroticism with negative affect and of extraversion with positive affect [@costa1980], and the facet results in @sec-appraisal point the same way. A satisfaction indicator built from the share of dissatisfied workers therefore reflects emotional stability more, and one built from the share of very satisfied workers reflects extraversion more.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-asym
#| tbl-cap: "Where on the scale each trait acts: effects on the probability of being extremely satisfied and of being not satisfied (mean of countries)"
nsv <- function(v) with_med("not_satisfied", TOT[TOT$var == v, ])
tab <- data.frame(Trait = unname(tl[traits]),
  `Extremely satisfied: effect (pp)` = sapply(traits, function(v) pp(tmean(v))), `Countries +` = sapply(traits, tsig),
  `Not satisfied: effect (pp)` = sapply(traits, function(v) pp(mean(nsv(v)$estimate))), `Countries −` = sapply(traits, function(v) sum(nsv(v)$p < .05 & nsv(v)$estimate < 0)),
  `Ratio bottom / top` = sapply(traits, function(v) f2(bt_ratio(v))), `Ordered-probit ratio` = sapply(traits, function(v) f2(ord_ratio(v))),
  `Sum: countries + / −` = sapply(traits, function(v) paste0(tb(v, 1), " / ", tb(v, -1))), `Sum below ordered-probit sum` = sapply(traits, function(v) paste0(tb_below(v), " / ", nC)), check.names = FALSE)
fin(kb(tab, row.names = FALSE, align = "lcccccccc"), size = 7.5, wrap = setNames(as.list(rep("1.8cm", 8)), 2:9), "Source: PIAAC Cycle 2 public-use files (OECD, 2024). Effects: total effects from mediate() in percentage points per SD of the trait, linear probability models; countries significant at the 5% level. Ratio: minus the mean effect on not satisfied over the mean effect on extremely satisfied. Ordered-probit ratio: the same ratio from an ordered probit of the 1–5 score with the same controls, which is equal for all traits within a country. Sum: coefficient of the trait in a regression of 'extremely satisfied or not satisfied' on the traits, the pay decile and controls, weighted least squares; countries with a significantly positive / negative sum, and countries in which the sum is below the sum implied by the ordered probit.")
```

## Exposure: little of the premium goes through the job {#sec-exposure}

@fig-indirect splits each country's total effect into the ACMEs through the 5 blocks and the ADE, and @tbl-med gives the means across countries. For emotional stability, the ADE is `r pp(dmean("EMOS"))` percentage points, against a total effect of `r pp(tmean("EMOS"))`. The 5 blocks together carry `r pp(amean("all", "EMOS"), 2)` points (`r pc(medshare("EMOS"))`%), significant in `r npos("all", "EMOS")` of `r nC` countries. Job demands carry the largest part, `r pp(amean("demands", "EMOS"), 2)` points (positive and significant in `r npos("demands", "EMOS")` countries): emotionally stable workers report fewer demands, and demands lower satisfaction. Resources add `r pp(amean("resources", "EMOS"), 2)`, pay `r pp(amean("pay", "EMOS"), 2)` (`r npos("pay", "EMOS")` of `r nmed("pay", "EMOS")` countries), and skill underuse `r pp(amean("underuse", "EMOS"), 2)` (`r npos("underuse", "EMOS")` countries). The ACME through job characteristics is close to zero (`r pp(amean("job", "EMOS"), 2)`). H2a receives weak support: the demands pathway is regular but small.

Extraversion has the largest pathway through the job. The ACME through resources is `r pp(amean("resources", "EXTR"), 2)` points and positive and significant in `r npos("resources", "EXTR")` of `r nC` countries, so H2b is supported for resources. Extraverts also report more demands and more skill underuse, and these ACMEs are negative (`r pp(amean("demands", "EXTR"), 2)` and `r pp(amean("underuse", "EXTR"), 2)`; significant in `r nneg("demands", "EXTR")` and `r nneg("underuse", "EXTR")` countries). Job characteristics add `r pp(amean("job", "EXTR"), 2)` and pay `r pp(amean("pay", "EXTR"), 2)`. The blocks together carry `r pc(medshare("EXTR"))`% of the extraversion effect. Conscientious workers also report more resources (`r npos("resources", "CONS")` countries). Open-mindedness shows the extraversion pattern more sharply: a positive ACME through resources (`r npos("resources", "OPEM")` countries) is offset by negative ACMEs through demands and underuse, and its direct effect is `r pp(dmean("OPEM"))` points. Agreeableness has almost no ACMEs; its effect is `r pc(dmean("AGRE") / tmean("AGRE"))`% direct.

```{r}
#| label: fig-indirect
#| fig-cap: "Causal mediation estimates by country: indirect effects of each trait through pay, job characteristics, job demands, job resources and skill underuse, and the direct effect, on the probability of being extremely satisfied. Bars to the right of zero raise the probability, bars to the left lower it; the parts add up to the total effect (circle, with 95% interval). Bottom row: means across countries. † No earnings decile released."
#| fig-height: 7.6
#| fig-width: 12
tv <- c("EMOS", "EXTR", "AGRE")
parts <- rbind(do.call(rbind, lapply(names(blk), function(m) { u <- AC[AC$mediator == m & AC$var %in% tv, ]
    data.frame(country = u$country, panel = tl[u$var], part = blk[[m]], value = 100 * u$estimate) })),
  { u <- ADE[ADE$var %in% tv, ]; data.frame(country = u$country, panel = tl[u$var], part = "Direct effect", value = 100 * u$estimate) })
tt <- TOT[TOT$var %in% tv, c("country", "var", "estimate", "se", "lower", "upper", "p")]; tt[c("estimate", "se", "lower", "upper")] <- 100 * tt[c("estimate", "se", "lower", "upper")]; tt$panel <- tl[tt$var]
fig_blocks_by_country(parts, tt, unname(tl[tv]), cname, flag, "Effect per SD of the trait (percentage points); circle = total effect, 95% interval")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-med
#| tbl-cap: "Causal mediation estimates: average causal mediation effect (ACME) of each trait through pay, job characteristics, job demands, job resources and skill underuse, average direct effect (ADE), and total effect on the probability of being extremely satisfied (mean of countries)"
fin(kb(med_table(names(blk), paste("ACME:", tolower(blk))), row.names = FALSE, align = "lccccc"), size = 8,
  sprintf("Source: PIAAC Cycle 2 public-use files (OECD, 2024). *** p < 0.01, ** p < 0.05, * p < 0.10. Output of mediate() (Tingley et al., 2014) from weighted linear mediator equations and a linear probability outcome equation (Imai, Keele & Yamamoto, 2010), estimated in each of the %d countries with %s quasi-Bayesian draws; entries are means of the country estimates in percentage points per SD of the trait, with the 95%% interval of the mean below. Each block enters as the index of its variables weighted by their coefficients in the outcome equation with all blocks; the block ACMEs add up to the indirect effect through all blocks. Pay: %d countries. Proportion mediated: sum of the block ACMEs over the total effect. Countries significant after adjustment: Table A20.", nC, big(med_info$sims), n_pay))
```

## Appraisal: the association is in the deviations {#sec-appraisal}

@tbl-split splits the ACMEs through demands and resources into the part through the occupational group's mean and the part through the worker's deviation from it. Nearly all of each ACME goes through the deviation. For emotional stability, the ACME through the deviations in demands is `r pp(amean("demands_dev", "EMOS"), 2)` points (positive and significant in `r npos("demands_dev", "EMOS")` of `r nmed("demands_dev", "EMOS")` countries), and that through the group means `r pp(amean("demands_mean", "EMOS"), 2)` (significant in `r npos("demands_mean", "EMOS") + nneg("demands_mean", "EMOS")` countries, either sign). Among the single conditions (Table A14), the deviation in time pressure carries most of it (`r npos("time_pressure_dev", "EMOS")` countries). For extraversion, the ACME through the deviations in resources is `r pp(amean("resources_dev", "EXTR"), 2)` (`r npos("resources_dev", "EXTR")` countries), mainly through voice, autonomy and learning, and that through the group means `r pp(amean("resources_mean", "EXTR"), 2)` (`r npos("resources_mean", "EXTR")` countries). Extraverts thus also work in groups that report more resources, but most of their pathway goes through the deviation.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-split
#| tbl-cap: "Group mean or individual deviation? ACME of each trait through the occupational-group mean and through the worker's deviation from it, by block of reported conditions (mean of countries)"
sl <- c(split_pay = "ACME: pay", split_job = "ACME: job characteristics", demands_mean = "ACME: job demands, group mean", demands_dev = "ACME: job demands, deviation",
  resources_mean = "ACME: job resources, group mean", resources_dev = "ACME: job resources, deviation", split_underuse = "ACME: skill underuse")
tb_ <- med_table(names(sl), unname(sl)); tb_ <- tb_[!tb_[[1]] %in% c("ADE: direct effect", "Total effect"), ]
fin(kb(tb_, row.names = FALSE, align = "lccccc"), size = 8, sprintf("Source: PIAAC Cycle 2 public-use files (OECD, 2024). *** p < 0.01, ** p < 0.05, * p < 0.10. Output of mediate() as in Table 3, %d countries (Austria and Germany release no occupation or industry codes); percentage points of the probability of being extremely satisfied per SD of the trait. Each reported condition is split into the weighted leave-one-out mean of the worker's occupation-by-industry group and the worker's deviation from it; each part enters as an index weighted by its coefficients in the outcome equation with all parts. Proportion mediated: over the total effect. Country estimates for each condition in Table A14.", n_a1))
```

@fig-perceived shows the trait coefficients on both parts of each condition. Emotionally stable workers report less time pressure than others in the same occupation and industry in `r pneg("time_pressure")` of `r n_a1` countries (sign test p `r fmtp(signp(pneg("time_pressure"), n_a1))`; significant in `r sum(perc("time_pressure")$p < .05 & perc("time_pressure")$estimate < 0)`). They also report less change, physical strain, learning, and social contact, each in at least `r min(sapply(c('change', 'physical', 'learning', 'social'), pneg))` of `r n_a1` countries. Less stable workers thus report higher demands and also more resources. Worse jobs, or a uniformly negative way of reporting, would raise demands and lower resources, so the pattern points to experiencing the same work as more intense. The coefficients on the group means are close to zero. For time pressure, the coefficient of emotional stability on the group mean is within ±`r eq_margin_cell` SD, with its 90% interval, in `r equiv(actsel("time_pressure"), eq_margin_cell)` of `r n_a1` countries (nominally significant in `r sum(actsel("time_pressure")$p < .05)`). Its minimum detectable effect is `r f3(2.8 * median(actsel("time_pressure")$se))` SD, against a typical deviation coefficient of `r f3(abs(median(perc("time_pressure")$estimate)))` SD. Extraverts report more voice, autonomy, learning, and social tasks than others in their group. The results are unchanged with minimum group sizes of 20 and 30 and with 1-digit occupations in every country (Table A5). H3a is supported. The design cannot exclude within-group differences in actual conditions that the occupation codes miss and that go in the same direction.

```{r}
#| label: fig-perceived
#| fig-cap: "Coefficients of emotional stability and extraversion on the worker's deviation from the occupational-group mean and on the group mean (SD per SD): cross-country mean with 95% interval; grey dots: countries. Right: countries significant at the 5% level (+/−). Austria and Germany excluded. Full results in Appendix, Table A15."
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-width: 11
row_m <- function(x, panel, item) { r <- summ(x)[1, ]
  data.frame(panel = panel, item = item, estimate = r$estimate, lower = r$lower, upper = r$upper,
    lab = count_label(sum(x$p < .05 & x$estimate > 0), sum(x$p < .05 & x$estimate < 0), nrow(x)), highlight = FALSE) }
ppn <- c("Emotional stability:\ndeviation", "Emotional stability:\ngroup mean", "Extraversion:\ndeviation", "Extraversion:\ngroup mean")
P <- do.call(rbind, lapply(conds, function(k) rbind(row_m(perc(k), ppn[1], cl[[k]]), row_m(actsel(k), ppn[2], cl[[k]]),
  row_m(perc(k, "EXTR"), ppn[3], cl[[k]]), row_m(actsel(k, "EXTR"), ppn[4], cl[[k]]))))
P$panel <- factor(P$panel, levels = ppn); P$item <- factor(P$item, levels = rev(unname(cl[conds])))
bgP <- do.call(rbind, lapply(conds, function(k) rbind(data.frame(panel = ppn[1], item = cl[[k]], estimate = perc(k)$estimate), data.frame(panel = ppn[2], item = cl[[k]], estimate = actsel(k)$estimate),
  data.frame(panel = ppn[3], item = cl[[k]], estimate = perc(k, "EXTR")$estimate), data.frame(panel = ppn[4], item = cl[[k]], estimate = actsel(k, "EXTR")$estimate))))
bgP$panel <- factor(bgP$panel, levels = ppn); bgP$item <- factor(bgP$item, levels = levels(P$item))
fig_means(P, "Mean coefficient across countries (SD of the condition per SD of the trait), 95% interval", band_last = FALSE, bg = bgP, x_pad = 0.55) + facet_wrap(~ panel, nrow = 1)
```

@fig-facets shows that low depression, the facet that measures sadness and low mood, accounts for the emotional-stability premium. Its coefficient is positive and significant in `r if (fsig("EMOS_DEPR") == n_fac) paste("all", n_fac) else paste(fsig("EMOS_DEPR"), "of the", n_fac)` countries with facet scores (mean `r pp(fmean("EMOS_DEPR"))` percentage points per SD). A stress-buffering account would single out low anxiety. Its coefficient is significant in `r fsig("EMOS_ANXI")` `r if (fsig("EMOS_ANXI") == 1) "country" else "countries"`. Low volatility is significant in `r fsig("EMOS_VOLA")`. The depression–anxiety difference is `r pp(fdiff("EMOS_DEPR-EMOS_ANXI")[["mean"]])` points on average (95% interval `r pp(fdiff("EMOS_DEPR-EMOS_ANXI")[["lo"]])` to `r pp(fdiff("EMOS_DEPR-EMOS_ANXI")[["hi"]])`) and significant in `r fdiff("EMOS_DEPR-EMOS_ANXI")[["pos"]]` of `r n_fac` countries. Within extraversion, energy, the facet closest to positive affect, has the largest coefficient (significant in `r fsig("EXTR_ENER")` countries). The facets associated with satisfaction are those closest to positive and negative affect, as H3b predicts. The low-depression facet measures a general tendency toward low mood and is not a clinical measure. Because it is close to evaluative well-being, the result suggests that the personality component of job satisfaction also relates to how people evaluate other life domains.

```{r}
#| label: fig-facets
#| fig-cap: "Coefficients of the 15 BFI-2 facets on the probability of being extremely satisfied (percentage points per SD), entered together with pay decile and controls, in the 12 countries with facet scores: cross-country mean with 95% interval; grey dots: countries. Right: countries significant at the 5% level (+/−). Country estimates in Appendix, Fig. A1."
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-width: 9
Fq <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(fl), function(f) { x <- FAo[FAo$var == f, ]; r <- summ(x)[1, ]
  data.frame(panel = tl[[sub("_.*", "", f)]], item = fls[[f]], estimate = 100 * r$estimate, lower = 100 * r$lower, upper = 100 * r$upper,
    lab = count_label(sum(x$p < .05 & x$estimate > 0), sum(x$p < .05 & x$estimate < 0), nrow(x)), highlight = FALSE) }))
Fq$panel <- factor(Fq$panel, levels = tl); Fq$item <- factor(Fq$item, levels = rev(unname(fls)))
bg <- data.frame(panel = factor(tl[sub("_.*", "", FAo$var)], levels = tl), item = factor(fls[FAo$var], levels = levels(Fq$item)), estimate = 100 * FAo$estimate)
fig_means(Fq, "Percentage points per SD of the facet, 95% interval", band_last = FALSE, bg = bg, x_pad = 0.3, label_at = max(bg$estimate) + 1) +
  facet_grid(panel ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y", switch = "y") +
  theme(strip.placement = "outside", strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1), strip.background = element_blank())
```

## Reactivity: small interactions between traits and reported conditions {#sec-reactivity}

@fig-reactivity shows all trait × condition products, with the 8 pre-specified ones outlined. Of the `r r_tested_n` country estimates of the pre-specified products, `r r_nom_tested` are significant at the 5% level, against `r round(0.05 * r_tested_n)` expected if all products were zero. The placebo products are significant in `r r_nom_placebo` of `r r_placebo_n` estimates, also more than the `r round(0.05 * r_placebo_n)` expected, so part of the excess is not specific to the hypotheses. Openness × learning has the predicted sign in `r rsum("R5")[["sameside"]]` of `r nC` countries (sign test p `r fmtp(signp(rsum("R5")[["sameside"]], nC))`) and extraversion × social tasks in `r rsum("R4")[["sameside"]]` (p `r fmtp(signp(rsum("R4")[["sameside"]], nC))`). Emotional stability × time pressure, the stress-buffering product, has the predicted sign in only `r rsum("R1")[["sameside"]]`. In a single country, I can detect only products of about `r pp(mde_med)` percentage points, as large as a condition's own slope. Of the country estimates, `r sum(sapply(tested, function(p) rsum(p)[["equiv"]]))` of `r r_tested_n` are equivalent to zero. The cross-country means are more precise. The largest is `r pp(max(abs(sapply(tested, function(p) rsum(p)[["mean"]]))))` points, against slopes of `r pp(csm[["autonomy"]])` points for autonomy, `r pp(csm[["voice"]])` for voice, and `r pp(csm[["time_pressure"]])` for time pressure. H4 is not supported in the sense of large moderation. Small moderation for openness and extraversion in the predicted direction remains compatible with the data. Table A16 gives the full results.

```{r}
#| label: fig-reactivity
#| fig-cap: "All trait × condition products: change in a condition's slope on the probability of being extremely satisfied per SD of the trait (percentage points per SD × SD), mean of country estimates; each product estimated in a model with all conditions. Below the mean: countries with p < 0.05 / countries estimated. Outlined: the 8 pre-specified products (H4); the 3 placebo products are among the others."
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-width: 10
PR <- CH[CH$model == "PROD" & CH$kind == "prod" & CH$outcome == o, ]; PR$trait <- sub(":.*", "", PR$var); PR$cond <- sub(".*:", "", PR$var)
cl_h <- c(cl[c("time_pressure", "repetitive", "physical", "change", "autonomy", "learning", "social", "support", "voice")], underuse = "Skill underuse")
H <- do.call(rbind, lapply(traits, function(v) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(cl_h), function(k) { u <- PR[PR$trait == v & PR$cond == k, ]
  data.frame(trait = tl[[v]], condition = cl_h[[k]], estimate = 100 * mean(u$estimate), n_sig = sum(u$p < .05), n = nrow(u)) }))))
H$trait <- factor(H$trait, levels = rev(tl)); H$condition <- factor(H$condition, levels = unname(cl_h))
ol <- pair_def[pair_def$sign != 0, ]; ol <- data.frame(trait = factor(tl[ol$trait], levels = rev(tl)), condition = factor(cl_h[ol$condition], levels = unname(cl_h)))
fig_heatmap(H, ol, fmt = "%.2f", unit = "pp per SD x SD")
```

## Composition: what the personality mix of worker groups changes {#sec-indicator}

@fig-gap shows the gap in the probability of being extremely satisfied between the high and low occupational groups in the `r n_ind` countries with occupation codes and at least 100 employees in each group. The raw gap is `r pp(mean(gap("raw")$estimate))` percentage points on average (range `r rng(100 * gap("raw")$estimate, 1)`) and significantly positive in `r sum(gap("raw")$p < .05 & gap("raw")$estimate > 0)` countries. When I standardize both groups to the pooled personality distribution, the gap falls by `r pp(median(abs(gap_change("raw", "standardised"))))` points at the median across countries (largest change `r pp(max(abs(gap_change("raw", "standardised"))))`), to `r pp(mean(gap("standardised")$estimate))` on average. Personality composition therefore accounts for `r pc(median(abs(gap_change("raw", "standardised")) / abs(gap("raw")$estimate)))`% of the gap at the median. When I add the pay decile, the gap becomes `r pp(mean(gap("traits_pay")$estimate))` points. When I also add reported conditions, it falls to `r pp(mean(gap("traits_pay_conditions")$estimate))`. Pay and conditions account for most of the gap. Personality accounts for a smaller part, as H5 predicts.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gap
#| fig-cap: "Gap in the probability of being extremely satisfied between managers and professionals (ISCO 1–2) and operative and elementary occupations (ISCO 8–9): raw, with both groups standardized to the pooled personality distribution, then adding the pay decile and the core reported conditions. Croatia and New Zealand use occupational skill levels; Ireland is excluded. Markers and † as in Fig. 2."
#| fig-height: 6.8
#| fig-width: 12
gl <- c(raw = "Raw gap", standardised = "Personality-\nstandardized", traits_pay = "+ pay decile", traits_pay_conditions = "+ pay and\nconditions")
u <- IND[IND$var %in% names(gl), c("country", "var", "estimate", "se", "lower", "upper", "p")]; u[c("estimate", "se", "lower", "upper")] <- 100 * u[c("estimate", "se", "lower", "upper")]; u$panel <- gl[u$var]
fig_country_dots(u, unname(gl), cname, flag, "Gap between the high and the low occupational group (percentage points), 95% interval") + theme(strip.text = element_text(size = 9.5, lineheight = 0.9))
```

## Sensitivity and robustness {#sec-robust}

Following @oster2019, I assume that unobservables matter as much as the observed controls (δ = 1, Rmax = 1.3 × R²). Under this assumption, the emotional-stability coefficient remains positive in `r sum(OS$trait == "EMOS" & OS$beta_star > 0)` of `r nC` countries. Its mean is `r pp(mean(OS$beta_star[OS$trait == "EMOS"]))` percentage points against an observed `r pp(mean(OS$b_full[OS$trait == "EMOS"]))` (Table A17). @masten2022 show that a coefficient can change sign with far less confounding than it takes to reach zero, so this result describes sensitivity to a single assumption. When I condition on life satisfaction, I remove a reporting disposition and any effect of a good job on a good life, so the result is not a bound. With this control, the emotional-stability premium is significant in `r sum(LSL$var == "EMOS" & LSL$p < .05 & LSL$estimate > 0)` of `r nC` countries. In the `r n_ten` countries that release tenure, trait × long-tenure products are significant in `r sum(TEN$p < .05)` of `r nrow(TEN)` cases, `r sum(TEN$p < .05 & TEN$estimate > 0)` positive and `r sum(TEN$p < .05 & TEN$estimate < 0)` negative, so the trait associations show no consistent growth with tenure. An immediate or non-monotonic effect of the job on trait reports would not show in this test.

@fig-sens shows how the ACMEs of emotional stability respond to unobserved confounding of the mediators. The error correlation $\rho^*$ at which the ACME would be zero is `r f2(rho_last("pay"))` for pay alone on average and rises to `r f2(rho_last("underuse"))` when all 5 blocks are included. A factor that correlates only weakly with both the mediators and satisfaction could therefore account for the mediated part. A reporting disposition is one such factor.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sens
#| fig-cap: "Sensitivity of the mediation estimates to unobserved confounding of the mediators, from medsens() (emotional stability, probability of being extremely satisfied). Panel a: ρ*, the correlation between the errors of the mediator and outcome equations at which the ACME through the blocks up to the one named is zero, by country (in the 3 countries without earnings deciles, the blocks start with job characteristics); dashed line: mean of countries. Panel b: mean ACME across countries at each assumed error correlation, as a percentage of the mean ACME at ρ = 0."
#| fig-height: 7.5
#| fig-width: 11
bl <- c(pay = "Pay", job = "+ job characteristics", demands = "+ demands", resources = "+ resources", underuse = "+ skill underuse")
fig_sensitivity(RHO, GRID, cname, bl)
```

Other forms of the outcome give the same ordering of the traits (Table A18). With the 1–5 score treated as cardinal, the total effect of emotional stability is `r with_med("satisfaction_score", f3(tmean("EMOS")))` points and significant in `r with_med("satisfaction_score", tsig("EMOS"))` of `r nC` countries. Extraversion and agreeableness are significant in `r with_med("satisfaction_score", tsig("EXTR"))` and `r with_med("satisfaction_score", tsig("AGRE"))` countries, conscientiousness in `r with_med("satisfaction_score", tsig("CONS"))`, and open-mindedness in `r with_med("satisfaction_score", tsig("OPEM"))`. The 5 blocks carry `r with_med("satisfaction_score", pc(medshare("EMOS")))`% of the emotional-stability effect on the score and `r with_med("not_satisfied", pc(medshare("EMOS")))`% of its effect on being not satisfied, against `r pc(medshare("EMOS"))`% for the main outcome. In the ordered probit, emotional stability raises the probability of the top category significantly in `r ord_sig("top", "EMOS")` countries without the mediators and in `r ord_sig("top", "EMOS", 1, "all")` with all of them. For conscientiousness, the counts are `r ord_sig("top", "CONS")` and `r ord_sig("top", "CONS", 1, "all")`, and for open-mindedness `r ord_sig("top", "OPEM")` and `r ord_sig("top", "OPEM", 1, "all")`. Logit marginal effects for being extremely satisfied are significant in `r lg("very_satisfied", "EMOS")`, `r lg("very_satisfied", "EXTR")`, `r lg("very_satisfied", "AGRE")`, `r lg("very_satisfied", "CONS")`, and `r lg("very_satisfied", "OPEM")` countries for the 5 traits, as in the linear probability model.

The baseline premiums are also unchanged with literacy instead of numeracy, with the 6-item trait scales, with a tenure control, and with the self-employed included (Table A19). When the job characteristics enter as controls rather than mediators, the mean emotional-stability coefficient is `r pp(kmean("EMOS", KJ))` percentage points against `r pp(kmean("EMOS", Ks))` in the baseline with the pay decile. Adding self-rated health, living with a partner, and having children lowers it to `r pp(kmean("EMOS", KCL))`, significant in `r kp5("EMOS", u = KCL)` countries. Self-rated health is itself related to emotional stability, so this last model removes part of the premium by construction.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

The subjective reward to non-cognitive skills is large compared with the objective one. For 1 standard deviation of emotional stability, the satisfaction premium is about `r pc(mean(PC$emos) / mean(PC$top_vs_bottom))`% of the within-country pay gradient in the probability of being extremely satisfied, and only `r pc(payshare("EMOS"))`% of the premium goes through pay. Wage returns estimated elsewhere, a few % of wages per standard deviation [@heckman2006; @almlund2011], are measured in different units and samples and cannot be compared directly. In the framework of @rosen1986, workers with these traits bring to any job a satisfaction premium equivalent to about a third of the pay gradient in satisfaction. In these data, little of this premium is reflected in pay. The results below suggest that it does not come from the jobs themselves either. On this interpretation, the subjective rewards to these skills exceed the objective ones. Personality is associated at least as strongly with intrinsic career success as with the extrinsic success measured by wages and employment.

The traits act at different ends of the satisfaction scale. Emotional stability works mainly at the bottom: it keeps workers out of the neutral and dissatisfied categories more than it moves them into the top one. Extraversion works mainly at the top. This division follows the link of neuroticism with negative affect and of extraversion with positive affect [@costa1980]. It also bears on measurement. Indicators of job quality that count dissatisfied workers and indicators that count very satisfied workers reflect different traits, so the choice between them changes which part of personality enters a comparison. Single-index models of the 1–5 score average the 2 ends and miss this division.

Little of the satisfaction premium is associated with better jobs (H2). Extraversion is a partial exception. Extraverts report more autonomy, learning, and voice, consistent with sorting into occupations with more influence and contact [@cobbclarkschurer2012; @oecd2025]. They also report more time pressure and skill underuse, and these pathways offset part of the gain from resources. Objective job characteristics such as occupation, hours, contract, and firm size carry almost none of the premium. Traits are linked to the jobs workers hold, but in these estimates the 5 blocks carry `r pc(medshare("EMOS"))`% of the emotional-stability premium and `r pc(medshare("EXTR"))`% of the extraversion premium.

Most of the reward is associated with how workers report their jobs (H3). The group means are equivalent across traits within a margin of a third of the deviation coefficient, and the part of the premium that moves with conditions moves with the deviations. The premium is concentrated in low depression, while low anxiety has little association with it. Negative affectivity has been treated either as a nuisance that inflates stressor–strain correlations or as a substantive trait that shapes exposure and reaction [@watson1984; @spector2000]. The results for the satisfaction premium suggest a third role, in which negative affectivity shapes how workers perceive their jobs, mainly through its depressive side. This study extends the diary and single-organization studies in that debate with representative data. Each worker's report is compared with an external reference point, the average report in that worker's occupation and industry.

Traits hardly change the association between conditions and satisfaction (H4). Contrary to trait activation theory [@tett2003] and person–environment fit [@kristofbrown2005], at the cross-country mean, the pre-specified products are small next to a condition's own slope. Given the power of the tests, I can exclude large moderation, but I cannot rule out small moderation in the predicted direction for openness and extraversion. In models of job amenities, workers may value conditions differently. Along personality lines, these valuation differences are small, at least for the conditions measured in this survey. The main effects of autonomy, learning, voice, time pressure, and skill underuse are large and similar for workers with different traits.

The reward also matters for comparisons between groups of workers (H5). About `r pc(median(abs(gap_change("raw", "standardised")) / abs(gap("raw")$estimate)))`% of the satisfaction gap between high and low occupational groups reflects their composition in these traits. At the same pay and conditions, the gap nearly closes. Comparisons of satisfaction across groups that differ in personality composition, by occupation, sex, age or health, include this component. Satisfaction gaps between groups of workers therefore combine unequal job quality with differences in the traits that shape how workers evaluate and report their work.

All variables are self-reported at a single point in time. A causal reading of the decomposition requires sequential ignorability. The appraisal results cast doubt on that assumption. Panel data with repeated measures of personality and conditions would establish temporal order [@maxwell2007]. Linked employer–employee data, with the workplace as the group, would distinguish a worker who sees the same job differently from one who holds a different job within the same codes. Regarding scale equivalence across languages, I rely on the instrument's validation [@soto2017].

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

Across `r nC` countries, emotionally stable, extraverted, and agreeable employees are more likely to be extremely satisfied with their jobs than other workers with the same pay and background. Conscientious employees are more likely to be extremely satisfied in `r tsig("CONS")` countries, and open-minded employees in `r tsig("OPEM")`, so the reward to these 2 traits depends on the labor market. Emotional stability acts mainly by keeping workers out of dissatisfaction, and extraversion by raising the share who are extremely satisfied. Pay, objective job characteristics, and reported working conditions carry little of the premium. It is associated mainly with how workers report their jobs and, within emotional stability, with low depression. Personality composition accounts for about `r pc(median(abs(gap_change("raw", "standardised")) / abs(gap("raw")$estimate)))`% of the satisfaction gap between broad occupational groups. `r pc(payshare("EMOS"))`% of the emotional-stability premium goes through pay, so workers with these traits are more satisfied mainly at the same level of pay. Non-cognitive skills are therefore associated with intrinsic as well as extrinsic career success.
